content.text: {"primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, a mountain primarily symbolizes the place of God's presence and divine revelation — the meeting point between heaven and earth where God discloses himself, gives covenant/law, and establishes his dwelling (his 'holy mountain,' Zion). By extension it frequently symbolizes God's kingdom or rule established over the earth.", "primary_basis": ["Exodus 3:1-12 (Horeb, the mountain of God, burning bush)", "Exodus 19-20; 24 (Sinai, giving of the Law, covenant)", "1 Kings 19:8-13 (Elijah meets God at Horeb)", "Psalm 48:1-2 (Zion, God's holy mountain)", "Psalm 2:6 ('I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill')", "Isaiah 2:2-4 and Micah 4:1-2 (the mountain of the LORD's house exalted above all mountains)", "Ezekiel 28:14 (the holy mountain of God)", "Matthew 5:1 (Sermon on the Mount)", "Matthew 17:1-8; Mark 9:2-8; Luke 9:28-36 (Transfiguration on a high mountain)", "Matthew 28:16-20 (Great Commission given on a mountain)", "Hebrews 12:18-24 (Sinai contrasted with Mount Zion, the heavenly Jerusalem)", "Revelation 21:10 (the new Jerusalem seen from a great, high mountain)"], "alternatives": [{"meaning": "Kingdoms, governments, or earthly powers — mountains as symbols of political/imperial authority, whether God's kingdom or hostile kingdoms to be brought low.", "basis": ["Daniel 2:35, 44-45 (the stone becomes a great mountain filling the earth)", "Jeremiah 51:24-25 (Babylon as a 'destroying mountain')", "Isaiah 41:15 (threshing mountains)", "Revelation 17:9-10 (seven mountains = seven kings in many readings)", "Isaiah 2:2 (mountain of the LORD exalted above all mountains, read as kingdom over kingdoms)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Obstacles, difficulties, or seemingly impossible problems that faith and prayer can overcome ('faith that moves mountains') — very widespread in devotional and popular preaching.", "basis": ["Matthew 17:20; 21:21", "Mark 11:22-23", "1 Corinthians 13:2", "Zechariah 4:7 ('Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain')", "Isaiah 40:4; Luke 3:5 (every mountain made low)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Stability, permanence, and unshakable security — often applied to God's faithfulness or the believer's trust.", "basis": ["Psalm 125:1-2 ('Those who trust in the LORD are like Mount Zion, which cannot be moved')", "Psalm 36:6 (righteousness like the mountains of God)", "Isaiah 54:10 (mountains may depart, but God's steadfast love will not)"], "prominence": "common"}, {"meaning": "Human pride, arrogance, or exaltation destined to be humbled before God.", "basis": ["Isaiah 2:12-14 (a day against all that is lofty, against the high mountains)", "Isaiah 40:4 (every mountain and hill made low)"], "prominence": "minority"}, {"meaning": "Places of false or idolatrous worship ('high places'), a negative cultic association.", "basis": ["Deuteronomy 12:2", "1 Kings 14:23; 2 Kings 17:10-11", "Jeremiah 3:6; Ezekiel 6:13", "Hosea 4:13"], "prominence": "minority"}], "has_settled_consensus": true, "confidence": "high", "notes": "Mountains are polyvalent in Scripture, and standard reference works (e.g., Dictionary of Biblical Imagery) list multiple senses. Nevertheless, the dominant and most widely taught symbolic meaning is the mountain as the site of divine encounter, revelation, and God's dwelling/kingdom (Sinai and Zion being the two paradigmatic mountains, taken up christologically in the Gospels and Hebrews). The 'kingdom/government' reading (Daniel 2; Isaiah 2) is especially prominent in prophetic and eschatological interpretation and in some charismatic/dominionist streams; the 'obstacle to faith' reading dominates popular devotional usage but is derived from specific sayings of Jesus rather than the broader biblical pattern. Context determines which sense applies in any given passage, but recognizable consensus on the primary theological symbolism (divine presence/revelation, Zion/kingdom) is well established."}
